nameStory: This plant earned its name 'evening-primrose' because its bright yellow flowers have a magical habit of opening in the evening, often right before your eyes! The blooms stay open through the night to attract nocturnal pollinators like moths, then close again by morning. It's like nature's own time-lapse show happening in slow motion.
description: Common evening-primrose is a tall, sturdy wildflower that can grow 3-5 feet high with a single main stem. It produces bright yellow, four-petaled flowers that bloom from bottom to top along the stem throughout summer. The plant has a rosette of leaves at its base and alternating leaves up the stem, giving it a somewhat weedy but cheerful appearance in fields and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four heart-shaped petals and a distinctive cross-shaped stigma in the center. Flowers are about 1-2 inches across and have a sweet, lemony fragrance that's strongest in the evening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy and are arranged alternately up the stem. The leaves have prominent white veins and may have small teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a tall spike with flowers opening from bottom to top over many weeks. The main stem is thick, sturdy, and often has a reddish tinge, especially near the base.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed capsules that split open lengthwise to reveal tiny dark seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken and persist on the dried stems through winter.

habitat: Look for common evening-primrose in disturbed soils like roadsides, old fields, vacant lots, and prairie edges throughout New England. It thrives in sunny spots with well-drained soil and seems to particularly enjoy gravelly or sandy areas where other plants struggle.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as fuzzy rosettes of leaves close to the ground. First-year plants spend the season building up energy in their taproot.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular bloom period when tall flower spikes appear and flowers open evening after evening from June through August. This is when the plant is most easily identified.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and long seed capsules develop. The plant begins to turn brown but capsules continue to ripen and split open to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stalks with empty seed capsules persist above snow, making gentle rattling sounds in winter winds. The distinctive capsule shape can still help with identification.

funFact: Evening-primrose flowers can actually open fast enough to watch with the naked eye - in just a few minutes on warm evenings, you can see the petals unfurl like nature's own time-lapse video, sometimes accompanied by an audible 'pop' as the flower buds burst open!
confusionNotes: The four-petaled yellow flowers distinguish it from most other tall yellow wildflowers like goldenrod (which has tiny clustered flowers) or wild parsnip (which has umbrella-shaped white flower clusters). Remember: four heart-shaped petals = evening-primrose family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, evening-primrose is not related to garden primroses at all - it's in a completely different plant family. The name comes purely from the evening blooming habit. This plant is also the source of evening primrose oil, which is extracted from the seeds and sold as a health supplement.
compareHints: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers. Small sundrops stay much shorter and bloom during the day, while northern evening-primrose has much smaller, pale yellow flowers. If you see big, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers on a tall plant, it's almost certainly common evening-primrose.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
